turns.doctor_question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, I came in because I just feel like I absolutely cannot get my schoolwork and my little accessories shop organized at the same time. It's a complete mess. My supplies, my due dates for classes, receipts, assignment notes... they literally all just end up in these huge piles everywhere and I never know what to do first. 

Like, just yesterday I was trying to sort out these new charms I got for the shop—they're these really cute little enamel frogs? I found them on this wholesale site, and usually their shipping takes absolutely forever, but they actually came early this time. Which was nice, except the mail carrier left the box right in front of my door and I literally tripped over it when I was leaving to get an iced coffee. I always go to that little drive-thru place down the street because their crushed ice is just the best, you know? I can't stand when places use those big blocky ice cubes. 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, yeah, so everything is just in piles and I really don't know where to start with it all.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they cannot get their schoolwork and shop organized, describing how supplies and notes end up in huge piles and they don't know where to start.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about enamel frogs, shipping, and iced coffee before losing their train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in elementary school, did you struggle with these same issues of organization and staying on task back then?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, elementary school... yeah. Actually, my mom still has all these old notes from my teachers back then. She keeps literally everything in this massive floral scrapbook she got at Michaels. I used to love going to Michaels with her when I was little because they have that whole aisle just for glass beads, and I'd make these little friendship bracelets for everyone in my class. I still have some of those beads, actually! They're mixed in with my shop supplies now, which is probably part of the whole pile problem I was just talking about... 

But wait, the notes! Right. Yeah, in the scrapbook, she saved all these teacher notes saying how I was constantly out of my seat, or like, blurting out answers and talking before they even called on me. And they always complained that I would rush through group activities. Like, I'd just speed right through the whole thing, even when I totally understood the work. I just couldn't sit there and wait for everyone else to finish, you know? We did this one group project on volcanoes in fourth grade and I ended up just doing the whole papier-mâché part myself because the paste smelled weird and I just wanted to get it over with so we could paint it. I painted mine with this neon orange glitter paint... wait, did you ask about middle school too, or just elementary?

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient references their 'whole pile problem' with their shop supplies, indicating ongoing difficulties with organization.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, going on tangents about a scrapbook, a craft store, and beads before remembering to answer the question.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient recalls elementary school teacher notes stating they were 'constantly out of my seat'.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient mentions that teachers complained about them 'blurting out answers and talking before they even called on me'.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient describes rushing through group activities because they 'couldn't sit there and wait for everyone else to finish'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you currently find that you have a hard time staying seated or feel like you are driven by a motor when you need to be still, such as during meetings or while working on your projects?
turns.patient_response:
Um, yeah, actually. It's really bad during my longer classes at the community college, or even if I have to sit through a vendor meeting on Zoom for the shop. I literally keep finding reasons to get up. Like, I'll suddenly need to check my inventory box to make sure I have enough jump rings, or I'll get up to refill my water bottle for the fifth time, or I'll just walk out into the hallway for a second. Staying in the chair just feels completely impossible after a while. 

Speaking of water bottles, I got this really cool insulated one recently that has all these holographic stickers on it. I spent like three hours arranging the stickers so they perfectly overlapped without covering up the designs. There's this one sticker of a little ghost drinking boba tea that is just my absolute favorite... but yeah, I just can't sit still for very long without feeling like I need to jump out of my skin.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they keep finding reasons to get up during classes and meetings because staying in the chair feels impossible.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense internal restlessness, stating they feel like they need to 'jump out of my skin' if they sit still for too long.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back over the last six months, would you say that these experiences of blurting out answers, feeling restless, or needing to get up from your seat happen frequently enough to be a daily struggle for you?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, it's definitely a daily thing. Honestly, it's been a huge problem for like, two years and two months now? Basically ever since I changed schools and started the business program, plus trying to run the shop at the same time. The new school just has way less structure, which you'd think would be great, right? Like, more freedom! 

I actually thought I was going to love it because they have this huge courtyard in the middle of the campus with these amazing willow trees. I love willow trees. When I was little, my grandma had one in her backyard and we used to pretend it was a secret fort. We'd take old blankets out there—she had this one specific quilt that was made entirely out of old denim jeans, which is such a cool upcycling idea, honestly. I've been thinking about trying to make little denim pouches for my shop to put the accessories in instead of those plastic baggies, because it's way more sustainable. I saw this tutorial on TikTok where this girl was turning thrifted jeans into... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the daily struggle thing. But yeah, since I changed schools and lost all that structure, it's just been a constant everyday issue trying to manage it all.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility in real-time by going off on a long tangent about willow trees, denim quilts, and TikTok before forgetting the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient confirms that needing to get up from their seat is a 'daily thing' and a 'constant everyday issue'.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms that feeling restless is a 'daily thing' and a 'constant everyday issue'.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient confirms that blurting out answers is a 'daily thing' and a 'constant everyday issue'.

turns.doctor_question: When you are in those classes or meetings, would you say that your need to move around or your tendency to blurt out answers happens almost every single time you are in those situations, or is it something that happens only occasionally?
turns.patient_response:
Um, yeah, it's pretty much every time. Especially the blurting out part. Like, if we're doing group critiques in my design class or just regular discussions, I just... I jump in with my answer before the other person is even done talking. It's like I already know what they're going to say, so I just say it for them. And then I always feel so embarrassed afterward because I realize I just totally guessed what they were getting at and cut them off. 

It's kind of like how I used to finish my sister's sentences when we were kids. She hated that so much. She actually threw a hairbrush at me once because I wouldn't stop doing it while she was trying to tell a story about her middle school crush. It was this guy named Tyler who always wore these really bright neon windbreakers. Like, the kind from the 90s that make that swoosh-swoosh sound when you walk? I actually love that sound. I found a jacket just like it at a thrift store last week, but it was missing a button, so I bought these vintage brass buttons to fix it. I have this whole jar of vintage buttons... wait, sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, the critiques. But yeah, it happens almost every single time I'm in a discussion.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, going on a tangent about windbreakers and vintage buttons before losing her train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states she jumps in with her answer before the other person is done talking during discussions.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient describes cutting others off and finishing their sentences, which constitutes interrupting.
